entry.title: Mechanics II: Symmetry and Conservation Laws
entry.content:
Mechanics II: Symmetry and Conservation Laws

In the previous article, we developed the basic framework of classical mechanics from the principle of least action. By varying the action, we obtained the Euler–Lagrange equations. We then used the properties of inertial frames to determine the Lagrangian of a free particle. This led us to momentum, potential energy, and force, and we derived Newton’s three laws in turn from the equations of motion. Along the way, we began to encounter conservation laws. The Lagrangian of a free particle has no explicit dependence on its position coordinates, so its momentum is conserved. Going from a single particle to a closed system, we found that the total momentum of the system is also conserved. These results bring us back to the question left open in the previous article. To see where conservation laws come from, we need to look beyond particular equations of motion and turn to symmetry. From that perspective, conservation laws that once seemed unrelated reveal a common origin.

Symmetry and Conservation Laws

However broadly or narrowly we define symmetry, it “is one idea by which man through the ages has tried to comprehend and create order, beauty, and perfection.”

— Symmetry [1]

In everyday language, “symmetry” often suggests balance, harmony, and beauty. It is widespread in nature and has influenced art and architecture as an aesthetic principle. In physics, we can describe symmetry in terms of transformations. For example, rotate a square by (90^\circ) about its centre or reflect it across one of its axes of symmetry, and the resulting figure coincides with the original. In other words, symmetry is the property of remaining unchanged under a transformation. The laws of nature can also exhibit this kind of invariance. In an inertial frame, for example, a free particle moves in a straight line at constant velocity. If we translate its entire trajectory in space or change the origin of time, the equations describing its motion retain the same form.

Mathematically, we define symmetry in terms of a transformation. Consider the field φ(x) under the coordinate transformation xa→xa−δxa .

We use a minus sign in the coordinate transformation so that the resulting expression for δφ has a plus sign. This discussion draws on Tong’s lecture notes [2].

The field value originally at x moves to x′ under the translation, so φ′(x′)=φ(x) . To evaluate the transformed field at the coordinate (x), we return to the original field at x+δx .

φ′(x)=φ(x+δx)

We can use this to calculate the change in the field.

δφ(x)=φ(x+δx)−φ(x)=δxa∂aφ+O(δx2)

To first order, this gives

δφ(x)=δxa∂aφ

To establish whether a transformation is a physical symmetry, we ask whether the physical laws remain unchanged under it. As discussed in the previous article, if a transformation adds only a total time derivative to the Lagrangian, it adds only an endpoint term to the action. With the endpoints held fixed, this term does not affect the variation of the action, so the equations of motion remain unchanged.

L(q˙+ϵ)−L(q˙)=ddtf(q,t)

This is the infinitesimal change δL in the Lagrangian. We can generalise the total time derivative to a total divergence. If the first-order change in the Lagrangian density under the transformation satisfies

δL=∂afa

then the action changes by at most a boundary term. The symmetries discussed below satisfy this condition.

Let the action over the spacetime region M be

S[φ]:=∫MdnxL[φ(x),∂aφ(x),x]

The symmetry condition gives the first-order change in the action.

δ∫MdnxL=∫MdnxδL=∫Mdnx∂afa

We can also vary the action directly.

δ∫MdnxL=∫MdnxδL=∫Mdnx[∂L∂φδφ+∂L∂(∂aφ)∂aδφ]=∫Mdnx[(∂L∂φ−∂a∂L∂(∂aφ))δφ+∂a(∂L∂(∂aφ)δφ)]

When the field satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equations, the first term vanishes, leaving the second term.

δ∫MdnxL=∫Mdnx∂a(∂L∂(∂aφ)δφ)

Comparing the two expressions pointwise gives

∫Mdnx∂a(∂L∂(∂aφ)δφ−fa)=0

We can then define the Noether current.

∂aJa=0Ja:=∂L∂(∂aφ)δφ−fa

Once a coordinate system is chosen, we can write the equations in components.

This is Noether’s theorem. It states that every continuous global variational symmetry of the action has an associated Noether current whose divergence vanishes when the field satisfies its equations of motion. Noether’s theorem is a central result of theoretical physics. It tells us that every continuous symmetry has a corresponding conservation law [3].

Emmy Noether was a German mathematician. Several prominent scholars have described her as the greatest woman mathematician in history. In physics, the theorem she proved revealed the close connection between symmetries and conservation laws. It is one of the most important theorems in the development of modern physics. [4]

Noether’s theorem gives the continuity equation ∂μJμ=0 . Integrating it over the spacetime region M gives

∫Mdnx∂μJμ=0

Let M=[t1,t2]×Σ , where the spatial region Σ does not change with time. We can therefore separate the time and space integrals. Taking the time derivative outside the spatial integral and applying the divergence theorem to the spatial divergence gives

∫t1t2dt∫Σdn−1x(∂0J0+∂iJi)=∫t1t2dt[∂0∫Σdn−1xJ0+∫Σdn−1x∂iJi]=∫t1t2dt[ddt∫Σdn−1xJ0+∫∂ΣdSiJi]

Here dSi is oriented along the outward normal. Since t1 and t2 can be chosen arbitrarily, the expression in square brackets vanishes at every instant.

ddt∫Σdn−1xJ0+∫∂ΣdSiJi=0

If the net flux through the boundary ∂Σ vanishes, then

dQdt=ddt∫Σdn−1xJ0=0Q:=∫Σdn−1xJ0

Q is the conserved charge associated with the symmetry.

A simple example can help us understand conserved currents and charges. Imagine a house with three rooms, A , B , and C , each connected to the other two. People can move between the rooms, and no one enters or leaves the house. Over a given interval, count the crossings from A to B and subtract the crossings from B to A . Call the net count Jμ . Similarly, let Jν and Jσ be the net crossing counts from B to C and from C to A , respectively. The change in the number of people in each room equals the number of inward crossings minus the number of outward crossings. Dividing by Δt gives the average rate of change in each room’s population.

ΔNAΔt=Jσ−JμΔtΔNBΔt=Jμ−JνΔtΔNCΔt=Jν−JσΔt

Adding the three equations, each net crossing count appears as an outflow for one room and an inflow for another, so the terms cancel. If N is the total number of people in the house, we obtain

ΔNΔt=0.

In this analogy, the time component J0(i) of the Noether current corresponds to the number of people in room i at a given instant.

J0(i)={NAi=ANBi=BNCi=C

The spatial components of the Noether current describe flow across a boundary. Here Jμ , Jν , and Jσ correspond to the accumulated net flux through the respective doorways over the interval of observation. The spatial integral in the continuous case becomes a sum over the three rooms. The resulting conserved charge Q=NA+NB+NC is the total number of people in the house.

Conservation Laws

Examples from Classical Mechanics

Consider a few examples from classical mechanics. We begin with spatial translations. In the chosen inertial frame, set x0=t and write the translation as xμ→xμ+aμ , with aμ constant. Since this is a purely spatial translation, a0=0 , so δxμ=aμ and δt=0 . A spatial translation leaves the velocity unchanged, so δx˙i=0 . Only the position term contributes to the first-order change in the Lagrangian, which satisfies the symmetry condition.

δL=aν∂νL=∂ν(aνL)fμ:=aνδ νμL

In classical mechanics, the coordinate x takes the place of the field φ , and the current has only the component μ=0 . To construct the conserved current, let i=1,2,3…;i≠0 .

J0=∂L∂x˙iai−aiδ i0L=∂L∂x˙iai

Since ai is constant, conservation of J0 means that the component of momentum along the direction of translation is conserved. A free particle has translational symmetry in all three independent spatial directions, so each momentum component satisfies

ddtpi=ddt∂L∂x˙i=0

We can use the same method to examine spatial rotations. If we choose the angle θ about a fixed axis as a coordinate, a rotation acts as a translation of θ . As with a spatial translation, the corresponding conserved quantity takes the form of a conjugate momentum, pθ=∂L/∂θ˙ . This is the component of angular momentum along the rotation axis. To see how angular momentum depends on position and momentum, we now switch to Cartesian coordinates. In these coordinates, a rotation of the position vector is written as

x′=R(θ)x

For an infinitesimal rotation, write the rotation angle as a vector δθ pointing along the rotation axis. The first-order change in position can be written using the Levi-Civita symbol.

δxμ=ϵμνσδθνxσ

Strictly speaking, μ should be an upper index. In Euclidean space, we can use the metric to raise or lower it, giving ϵ νσμ=ϵμνσ .

Suppose this spatial rotation satisfies the symmetry condition. Substituting into the expression for the conserved current gives

J0=∂L∂x˙iδxi−δxiδ i0L=∂L∂x˙iδxi

Equivalently, we have

J0=piϵiνσδθνxσ:=Lνδθν

Since δθν is constant, the continuity equation gives

ddtLν=0

Writing out the individual components gives

L1=x2p3−x3p2L2=x3p1−x1p3L3=x1p2−x2p1

Putting the components together in vector form gives conservation of the total angular momentum.

L=x×p=const.

We can examine time-translation symmetry in much the same way. As in the spatial case, we now consider the translation t0→t0+τ0 .

J0=∂L∂x˙ix˙iτ0−Lτ0ddt[∂L∂x˙ix˙i−L]=0

The conserved quantity associated with time translations is energy. As an example in one dimension, suppose a particle moves in a potential V(x) , with Lagrangian

L=12mx˙2−V(x)

Substituting into the expression for energy gives

E=∂L∂x˙ix˙i−L=mx˙2−12mx˙2+V(x)=12mx˙2+V(x)

The particle’s kinetic and potential energies add up to a constant. This is the familiar law of conservation of mechanical energy.

Energy–Momentum Tensor

Canonical Energy–Momentum Tensor

In the previous section, we considered spatial and temporal translations separately in classical mechanics. We now apply the same idea to field theory, treating both as spacetime translations. Following the earlier convention, take x′a=xa−ξa , where ξa is constant. When the Lagrangian density has no explicit dependence on the spacetime coordinates, the first-order changes in the field and its Lagrangian density are

δL=ξa∂aL=∂a(ξaL)δφ=ξa∂aφ

The first-order change in the Lagrangian density is a total divergence. Substituting the variation of the field and the corresponding boundary term into the earlier expression for the Noether current gives

Ja=[∂L∂(∂aφ)∂bφ−δ baL]ξb

Each choice of translation direction gives an associated Noether current. Collecting the conserved currents for translations in all directions gives the canonical energy–momentum tensor.

Ja=Tabξb=TabηbcξcTab:=∂L∂(∂aφ)∂bφ−ηabL

Since ξa is constant and can be chosen independently along each spacetime direction, we have

∂a(Tabξb)=ξb∂aTab=0∂aTab=0

This is the conservation equation for the canonical energy–momentum tensor. We now examine its components in four-dimensional Minkowski spacetime, with ημν=diag(1,−1,−1,−1) .

The convention ημν=diag(−1,1,1,1) is also possible. We use the former metric signature to raise and lower indices throughout the discussion below.

Consider the component T00 . Since ∂0=∂0 , we have

T00=∂L∂(∂0φ)∂0φ−L=∂L∂φ˙φ˙−L

This expression gives the energy density of the field. Integrating over all of space Σ at a fixed time gives the total energy.

E=∫Σd3xT00

Next, consider T0i . Here ∂i=−∂i , so

T0i=∂L∂(∂0φ)∂iφ=−∂L∂φ˙∂iφ

Its physical meaning can be seen from the time component of the conserved current.

J0=T0μξμ

A pure time translation selects T00 , which is the energy density. A pure spatial translation along the i th coordinate direction selects T0i , the i th component of the momentum density. Integrating over all of space gives the corresponding component of the total momentum.

Pi=∫Σd3xT0i

Next, consider Ti0 .

Ti0=∂L∂(∂iφ)φ˙

For a pure time translation, it gives the spatial components of the corresponding conserved current.

Ji=Ti0ξ0

Expanding the time component of the conservation equation for the canonical energy–momentum tensor gives

∂tT00+∂iTi0=0

Since T00 is the energy density, Ti0 is the energy flux density along the i th coordinate direction. We denote its volume integral over the spatial region Σ by

ei=∫Σd3xTi0

Finally, the purely spatial components of the energy–momentum tensor are

Tij=−∂L∂(∂iφ)∂jφ−(−δij)L=δijL−∂L∂(∂iφ)∂jφ

For a pure spatial translation, these components determine the spatial part of the corresponding conserved current.

Ji=Tijξj

Keeping the second index fixed, we can write the conservation equation as

∂tT0j+∂iTij=0

Here T0j is the density of the j th component of momentum. Thus Tij is the flux density of the j th momentum component in the i th direction. For fixed j , we denote the volume integral of this flux density over the spatial region Σ by

pi=∫Σd3xTij

There is another way to interpret Tij . Integrating the conservation equation gives

∫Σd3x(∂tT0j+∂iTij)=0∫Σd3x∂tT0j=−∫Σd3x∂iTijddtPj=−∫Σd3x∂iTij=−∫∂ΣdSiTij

The rate of change of the j th momentum component within the region is the negative of the net outward flux through the boundary. This gives the connection between momentum flux density and stress. If traction is defined in terms of the force exerted by the boundary on the region inside, the stress components take the corresponding sign in the equation above. For a surface whose normal lies along the i th direction, i=j corresponds to normal stress and i≠j corresponds to shear stress.

ComponentSymmetryExpressionPhysical meaning
T00 Time translation ∂L∂φ˙φ˙−L Energy density
T0i Spatial translation −∂L∂φ˙∂iφ Momentum density
Ti0 Time translation ∂L∂(∂iφ)φ˙ Energy flux density
Tij Spatial translation δijL−∂L∂(∂iφ)∂jφ Momentum flux density

This section draws on [2] [5].

Energy–Momentum Tensor

We can extend this idea to a manifold (M,gab) equipped with a metric and describe spacetime symmetries in terms of isometries of the metric. Suppose there is a vector field ξa along whose flow the metric remains unchanged, so that

Lξagab=0

We then call it a Killing vector field [6]. The Minkowski spacetime translations considered above provide an example. Given a tensor Tab and a Killing vector field ξa , we can construct

Ja=Tabξb

Taking its covariant divergence gives

∇a(Tabξb)=(∇aTab)ξb+Tab∇aξb

The Killing equation ∇(aξb)=0 tells us that the symmetric part of ∇aξb vanishes. Decomposing the second term into its symmetric and antisymmetric contributions gives

(∇aTab)ξb+Tab∇aξb=(∇aTab)ξb+T(ab)∇(aξb)+T[ab]∇[aξb]=(∇aTab)ξb+T[ab]∇[aξb]

Let us return to the case of flat spacetime. The canonical energy–momentum tensor obtained from spacetime translation symmetry obeys the conservation equation, and the covariant derivative of the constant vector field generating the translation vanishes. Thus

∇aTab=0∇aξb=0

We therefore have a conserved current.

∇aJa=0

In the spacetime translations discussed above, the generating vector field ξa was constant. In inertial coordinates in Minkowski spacetime, ∇aξb=0 , so the conservation equation ∇aTab=0 is enough to give the conserved current Ja=Tabξb . For more general isometries, the generating Killing vector field may have ∇aξb≠0 . As the preceding calculation shows, even when ∇aTab=0 , the divergence of the current may still contain the term

∇aJa=T[ab]∇[aξb]

If this term is nonzero, the current is not conserved. If Tab is symmetric, its antisymmetric part T[ab] vanishes. We therefore seek a new energy–momentum tensor that is symmetric and obeys the original conservation equation. One way to do this is to add a divergence term to the canonical energy–momentum tensor [6]. Introduce a tensor Bcab satisfying

{Bcab=−Bacb∇cBc[ab]=−T[ab]∇a∇cBcab=0

We define the modified canonical tensor and call it the energy–momentum tensor.

Tnewab:=Tab+∇cBcab

First, let us see how the correction makes the tensor symmetric. Taking the antisymmetric part in (a,b) gives

Tnew[ab]=T[ab]+∇cBc[ab]=T[ab]−T[ab]=0

Next, consider the conservation equation. Taking the covariant divergence of the new tensor gives

∇aTnewab=∇aTab+∇a∇cBcab=∇aTab

If the original tensor satisfies ∇aTab=0 , the new tensor does as well. We can then construct a new conserved current.

Jnewa=Tnewabξb

It satisfies

∇aJnewa=0

In this way, for every continuous isometry of the metric generated by a Killing vector field, we can construct the corresponding conserved current from the same improved energy–momentum tensor.

This section draws on [6].

The Significance of Noether’s Theorem

“Pure mathematics is, in its way, the poetry of logical ideas.” Einstein goes on to describe the search for general operations that gather as many formal relationships as possible into a simple, logical whole. In pursuing this logical beauty, mathematicians find conceptual tools that let us probe the laws of nature more deeply.

— Einstein’s tribute to Noether [7]

Noether’s theorem changed how we understand physical laws. It did more than add another result to theoretical physics. Before it, conserved quantities were often treated as empirical facts. The theorem brought them together as consequences of continuous symmetries. Time-translation symmetry corresponds to conservation of energy, spatial translation symmetry to conservation of momentum, and spatial rotation symmetry to conservation of angular momentum. This is how symmetry enters the laws governing conserved quantities in the motion of matter.

Noether’s theorem also changed how physicists build theories. Given a theory, we can start from its symmetries and identify conserved quantities before solving the equations of motion. In developing a new theory, we can reason in the other direction. We first determine what symmetries the theory has, then use them to decide which terms can appear in the action. From explaining conservation laws in classical mechanics to constraining theories of fundamental interactions, symmetry has become a starting point for building physical theories. As a matter of method, Noether’s theorem changed the way physicists work by making the search for symmetries a central part of constructing theories.

References

[1]
H. Weyl, Symmetry. Princeton University Press, 1952. doi: 10.1515/9781400874347.
[2]
D. Tong, “Quantum field theory,” University of Cambridge, Lecture notes, 2006–2007. Available: https://www.damtp.cam.ac.uk/user/tong/qft/one.pdf
[3]

[4]
“埃米·诺特.” Accessed: Nov. 14, 2026. [Online]. Available: https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%9F%83%E7%B1%B3%C2%B7%E8%AF%BA%E7%89%B9
[5]

[6]

[7]

entry.title: Mechanics I: The “Principles” and Equations of Motion
entry.content:
Mechanics I: The “Principle” and Equations of Motion

Inertial Frames

“What is an inertial system?”

“It is a c.s. in which the laws of mechanics are valid.”

— The Evolution of Physics [1]

Here, c.s. stands for co-ordinate system.

The inertial frame of reference, or inertial frame for short, provides the setting for mechanics and is a cornerstone of classical physics. An inertial frame is a frame of reference in which space can be described as homogeneous and isotropic, and time as homogeneous. Spatial homogeneity means that no position is privileged. Spatial isotropy means that no direction is privileged. Temporal homogeneity means that no instant is privileged. In other words, for an isolated system free from outside influences, changing the location, orientation, or starting time of the experiment as a whole should leave the laws of mechanics governing it unchanged.

Galileo’s inclined-plane thought experiment can help make this abstract idea more concrete. For now, let us set aside the causes of changes in motion and simply observe what a ball does. It speeds up as it rolls downhill and slows down as it rolls uphill. How, then, would it move on a level surface, where it neither climbs nor descends? Experiments show that the ball generally slows to a stop, but it tends to roll farther on a flatter, smoother surface. The distance it rolls therefore depends on the experimental conditions. Now place two inclined planes opposite each other and join them smoothly at the bottom. A ball released from rest on one side rolls down and then climbs the other side. As the experimental conditions improve, the height it reaches approaches its starting height. This suggests that if the impediments present in the actual experiment could be removed, the ball would rise to its original height on the other side. Now keep the release height fixed and gradually reduce the angle of the second incline. To reach the same height, the ball must travel farther and farther. Once the second surface is entirely level, the ball cannot regain its original height however far it travels, so it keeps moving. The thought experiment helps us understand that in an inertial frame, a free particle unaffected by other bodies remains at rest or moves in a straight line at constant velocity.

This is Newton’s first law, which also asserts that inertial frames exist.

Consider a second frame that moves at constant velocity relative to a known inertial frame, with no relative rotation of the coordinate axes. Observers in the two frames may record different velocities for the same object, but they agree on whether its velocity remains constant. The measured velocities differ only by the constant relative velocity of the frames. If the object moves in a straight line at constant speed in one frame, its velocity also remains constant in magnitude and direction in the other. The second frame therefore satisfies the condition for inertial motion and is itself an inertial frame. By contrast, in a non-inertial frame, even an object unaffected by other bodies need not remain at rest or move in a straight line at constant velocity. Viewed from a rotating platform, for example, a free object travelling in a straight line may appear to follow a curved path. Free motion alone gives us no way to single out a privileged inertial frame. Extending this equivalence to all the laws of mechanics gives Galileo’s principle of relativity. The laws of mechanics governing the same physical process have the same form in all inertial frames.

“The same” refers to the form of the laws. Observers in different frames may record different positions and velocities.

How can we determine whether a particular frame is inertial? A single direct measurement cannot fully establish the homogeneity and isotropy described above. We must observe the motion of objects, eliminate the effects of other bodies and the apparatus as far as possible, and check whether the observations agree with the law of inertia. Every experiment is limited in duration, spatial extent, and precision, so it cannot cover every possible case. Repeated experiments can test the applicability of inertial frames, within those limits. For the problems discussed in this part of the series, we can work in inertial frames throughout.

We take the existence of inertial frames as a starting point of the theory. This is also an essential part of Newton’s first law. Although we have yet to introduce the second law, treating the first merely as a special case of the second would overlook its role in the theory. Even if the second law yields uniform straight-line motion under a particular condition, its usual form already presupposes an inertial frame. Deriving that special case therefore cannot establish the existence of inertial frames.

Newton’s first law describes free motion and asserts that there are inertial frames in which bodies move this way, providing the basis for the dynamics that follows.

The “Principle” and Equations of Motion

“The fundamental laws can be put in the form of a principle of least action.”

— The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. II [2]

The principle of least action, referred to below as the principle, is widely used across physics. It offers a unified description by taking the entire trajectory over a time interval and using a quantity called the action to obtain the equations of motion. Laws of motion with different forms can thus be expressed within a single variational framework, illustrating the search for simplicity and unity in physics. In this article, we will approach mechanics through this principle.

“Least” is the traditional term. With the initial and final times and endpoint configurations fixed, any infinitesimal variation of the actual trajectory leaves the action unchanged to first order. The action is then said to be stationary.

The action is defined by

S=:∫t1t2Ldt

In other words, the action is the integral of the Lagrangian L over the given time interval. We write the Lagrangian as L(q,q˙,t) , where q denotes the generalised coordinates, q˙ the generalised velocities, and t time. Why is it enough to stop at velocity? Knowing where an object is now does not tell us what it will do next, since it can pass through the same position with different velocities. For the classical systems considered here, experience shows that once all the generalised coordinates and velocities are specified at one instant, the law of motion determines the subsequent motion. The same law determines the acceleration. In mathematical terms, the motion is governed by second-order differential equations. The variational derivation below shows that when a Lagrangian depends only on the coordinates and their first time derivatives, the resulting equations of motion contain at most second time derivatives of the coordinates.

What happens if we include acceleration in the Lagrangian? If the dependence on acceleration is nondegenerate, variation yields fourth-order equations of motion. To determine a trajectory, we must then specify the initial acceleration and its rate of change independently, in addition to the initial position and velocity [3]. The theory would therefore allow different trajectories with identical initial positions and velocities, depending on the values of those additional initial data. This conflicts with the observed behaviour of the systems considered here, so we use L(q,q˙,t) to describe their dynamics.

Now fix the initial and final times and the generalised coordinates at those times. Infinitely many candidate trajectories satisfy these conditions. Even two trajectories that follow the same path through space correspond to different functions q(t) if they trace it at different speeds. Substituting each candidate trajectory into the integral gives a value of the action. We therefore write the action as S[q] and call it a functional of the trajectory. What condition does the actual trajectory satisfy? According to the principle, if we hold the endpoint times and coordinates fixed and vary the actual trajectory infinitesimally, the first-order change in the action vanishes. The stationarity condition is

δS=0.

To calculate the variation of the action, we impose δt=0 and the endpoint conditions δq|t1=δq|t2=0 .

δ∫t1t2L(q,q˙,t)dt=∫t1t2δL(q,q˙,t)dt=∫t1t2∑α=1n(∂L∂qαδqα+∂L∂qα˙δqα˙+∂L∂tδt)dt=∫t1t2∑α=1n(∂L∂qαδqα+∂L∂qα˙δqα˙)dt

Integration by parts produces a total time derivative. Integrating it gives a boundary term that vanishes under the endpoint conditions.

∫t1t2∑α=1n(∂L∂qαδqα+∂L∂qα˙δqα˙)dt=∫t1t2∑α=1n[∂L∂qαδqα+ddt(∂L∂qα˙δqα)−ddt(∂L∂qα˙)δqα]dt=∫t1t2∑α=1n[∂L∂qαδqα−ddt(∂L∂qα˙)δqα]dt=∫t1t2∑α=1n[(∂L∂qα−ddt∂L∂qα˙)δqα]dt=0

The variations δqα are independent. For the equality to hold for all allowed variations, we must have

∂L∂qα−ddt∂L∂qα˙=0

This is the Euler–Lagrange equation. It provides a general method for obtaining the equations of motion from a Lagrangian. To apply it to a particular system, we still need to determine that system’s Lagrangian. Let us start with a free particle in an inertial frame. What quantities can its Lagrangian L depend on? Write its Cartesian position as q and its velocity as q˙ . Because time is homogeneous, releasing the particle at different times from the same position with the same velocity gives motion governed by the same law. Because space is homogeneous, changing the initial position while keeping the initial velocity fixed simply translates the trajectory. The starting time and position therefore make no difference to the law of free motion. Accordingly, we take the Lagrangian to depend only on velocity.

L=L(q˙)

Before determining its form, let us return to the variation of the action. The total time derivative produced by integration by parts can be integrated directly, leaving a term evaluated only at the endpoints. In deriving the Euler–Lagrange equation, this boundary term vanishes because the variations at the endpoints are zero. This suggests that we obtain the same equations of motion whenever we modify the action in a way that preserves its stationarity condition. One simple example is multiplying the entire Lagrangian by a nonzero constant k . Under L→kL , the variation of the action is multiplied by the same constant. Hence kδS=0 and δS=0 give the same equations of motion. Now let ϕ(q,t) be a sufficiently smooth function and add its total time derivative dϕ/dt to the Lagrangian. On integration, the change in the action depends only on the endpoint values of ϕ .

S⟶S+[ϕ(q,t)]t1t2=S+ϕ(q(t2),t2)−ϕ(q(t1),t1).

The initial and final times are fixed, and δq|t1=δq|t2=0 , so all the trajectories under comparison have the same endpoints. The added boundary term is consequently the same for each trajectory, and its variation vanishes.

L⇔L+ddtϕ(q,t)

The two Lagrangians give the same equations of motion and are equivalent as descriptions of the system’s dynamics.

Given that different Lagrangians can yield the same equations of motion, how should we choose one for a free particle? We have used the homogeneity of time and space to write it as L(q˙) . We now use Galileo’s principle of relativity to determine how it depends on velocity. Consider two inertial frames K and K′ whose axes are aligned. Suppose the transformation from K to K′ changes the particle’s velocity from q˙ to q˙+ϵ , where ϵ is a constant infinitesimal vector of arbitrary direction. We require that the transformation change the Lagrangian by at most a total time derivative. The action then changes only by a boundary term, so the stationarity condition and equations of motion are preserved.

L(q˙+ϵ)−L(q˙)=ddtϕ(q,t)

Expanding the first term on the left in powers of ϵ gives

L(q˙+ϵ)−L(q˙)=L(q˙)+∇L(q˙)Tϵ+12!ϵTH(q˙)ϵ+...−L(q˙)=∇L(q˙)Tϵ+12!ϵTH(q˙)ϵ+...=ddtϕ(q,t)

The right-hand side is a total time derivative and is therefore at most first degree in velocity. Comparing the terms of first order in ϵ shows that ∇LTϵ is also at most first degree in velocity. Since ϵ can point along any coordinate axis, the partial derivative of L with respect to each velocity component is at most first degree in the full velocity vector. Hence L is a polynomial of degree at most two in velocity.

L(q˙)=12q˙TMq˙+Bq˙+C

Here M is a constant symmetric matrix, B a constant row vector, and C a scalar constant. The last two terms together form a total time derivative.

Bq˙+C=ddt(Bq+Ct)

Dropping this term leaves the equations of motion unchanged. The free-particle Lagrangian therefore reduces to

L(q˙)=12q˙TMq˙

In Cartesian coordinates, spatial isotropy requires this quadratic form to have the same value for all velocities of equal magnitude. Evaluate it at velocities of the same magnitude along the eigenvectors of M . The resulting values can agree only if all the eigenvalues are equal. Thus M=mI , giving

L=T=12mr˙2

The coefficient m is the particle’s inertial mass. The expression above is the familiar kinetic energy, denoted by T . With the free-particle Lagrangian in hand, we write the particle’s position vector as r and substitute the Lagrangian into the equation of motion.

∂L∂qα−ddt∂L∂qα˙=0ddt(mr˙)=0

The particle’s mass m is constant, so its velocity vector r˙ is constant as well. This agrees with our earlier description of inertial motion. The equation also identifies a conserved quantity. To extend the idea to generalised coordinates, we define the conjugate momentum pα corresponding to qα by

pα:=∂L∂qα˙

In the Cartesian coordinates x , y , and z of a free particle, the conjugate momenta are mx˙ , my˙ , and mz˙ , respectively. These are the three components of the particle’s momentum p=mr˙ . The equation of motion shows that p stays constant throughout the motion. This is conservation of momentum for a free particle.

p=mr˙=const.

Why is momentum conserved? In terms of conjugate momentum, the Euler–Lagrange equation reads

dpαdt=∂L∂qα

If the Lagrangian does not explicitly depend on a coordinate qα , the right-hand side vanishes and the corresponding conjugate momentum remains constant. A translation of the free particle in any Cartesian direction leaves its Lagrangian unchanged, so all three components of its momentum are conserved. The conservation of momentum for a free particle is thus linked to spatial translation symmetry. Does this connection extend to other conservation laws? In the next article, we will use this question to explore the relationship between symmetries and conservation laws.

Having considered a free particle in an inertial frame, let us now see what happens when a particle is subject to an interaction. Take a fixed source as an example. Its effect on the particle may differ from one position to another. Moving the particle while leaving the source in place may therefore change the particle’s subsequent motion. For interactions that can be described by a function of position, we subtract a function V(q) , called the potential energy, from the free-particle Lagrangian.

L=T−V=12q˙TMq˙−V(q)

In Cartesian coordinates, the negative gradient of the potential energy with respect to position gives the force on the particle.

F=−∇V

The minus sign indicates that the force points in the direction of steepest decrease in potential energy. A force that can be written as the negative gradient of a time-independent potential energy is called conservative. For a single particle of constant mass, substituting L=T−V into the Euler–Lagrange equation gives F=mr¨ . This is the form Newton’s second law takes here. More generally, we can collect the effects of the interactions on the right-hand side of the equation and use the generalised force Fα to express their effect on the coordinate qα .

ddt∂T∂q˙α−∂T∂qα=Fα

In Cartesian coordinates, Fα is the corresponding component of the ordinary force. In other coordinates, its meaning depends on the choice of coordinates. If the interaction is described by a position-dependent potential energy, then Fα=−∂V/∂qα . In other cases, Fα is determined by the particular interaction.

Some velocity-dependent interactions can be included directly in the Lagrangian. Even a term linear in velocity can affect the equations of motion. If the term can be written as the total time derivative of a function, its integral changes only the boundary term in the action, so the term may be omitted.

Does our initial focus on interactions that can be represented by potential energy reveal a limit of the principle, given how often nonconservative forces occur in practice?

We can address this question by broadening our view from the objects we directly observe to the entire interacting system. Modern physics describes the fundamental interactions in nature in terms of gravity, electromagnetism, and the strong and weak interactions. In a particular mechanics problem, we generally consider only a few variables directly relevant to the motion under study. Energy can be transferred to degrees of freedom outside the model through microscopic motion or electromagnetic radiation, for example. The observed motion then exhibits dissipation, which can be described using nonconservative forces. The appearance of these forces is therefore related to how we define the system’s boundaries. The principle can be used to construct a more complete description of the dynamics, while nonconservative forces can account for processes that the simpler model leaves implicit.

Finally, consider an isolated system of two particles in an inertial frame. Suppose their interaction potential V depends only on their relative position r1−r2 . Adding the Euler–Lagrange equations for the two particles gives the rate of change of their total momentum.

ddt(p1+p2)=F1+F2

Since r1 and r2 appear with opposite signs in the relative position, the chain rule gives ∇r1V=−∇r2V . It follows that

F1+F2=−∇r1V−∇r2V=0

The particles’ total momentum is therefore conserved, and the forces they exert on each other are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. This is Newton’s third law.
